title: Spline Curves
body:
Given a set of points, draw a smooth curve through them. The naive answer is one polynomial of
high degree, and the naive answer is wrong. A **spline** is a chain of low-degree polynomials,
one per interval, glued together so the joins are invisible.

The name is literal: a draughtsman's spline was a thin flexible strip held down by weights, and
the curve it settles into is the one that minimises bending energy. Cubic splines are the
mathematics of that strip.

## Why not one polynomial

A single polynomial through $n$ points needs degree $n - 1$, and high-degree polynomials
oscillate wildly between their constraints. Runge's phenomenon: fit an innocent bell-shaped
function at evenly spaced points and the error near the edges *grows* as you add points. More
data makes it worse.

Two other things go wrong: the fit is global, so moving one point changes the entire curve, and
the coefficients become numerically horrible. Splines fix all three by keeping the degree fixed
at 3 and letting the number of *pieces* grow instead. See [[Taylor Series]] for the other way of
approximating a function locally, and note the difference: a Taylor series is exact at one point
and drifts; a spline is exact at every knot.

## Continuity classes

The joins are called **knots**, and the whole design question is how much agreement to demand
there. See [[Derivative]] in [[CALCULUS 1]]:

| Class | Matches at the knot | Looks like |
|---|---|---|
| $C^0$ | position | a kink, connected but corners |
| $C^1$ | position, first derivative | smooth direction, visible change in curvature |
| $C^2$ | position, first and second derivative | smooth to the eye, no visible seam |

**Cubic is the smallest degree that reaches $C^2$**, and that is the whole reason cubics are the
default. Count: $n$ intervals give $4n$ unknown coefficients. Interior knots supply position,
slope, and curvature agreement, endpoints supply their values, and two conditions are left over.
Setting the end curvature to zero gives the **natural spline** (the flexible strip going straight
past the last weight); fixing the end slopes gives the **clamped spline**.

## It is a linear system

The $C^2$ conditions are linear in the unknown coefficients, so solving for a cubic spline is
solving $Ax = b$, and $A$ is **tridiagonal**: each knot's equation involves only its two
neighbours. That is [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]], and the tridiagonal structure is why the solve is $O(n)$
rather than $O(n^3)$. Splines are cheap for the same reason they are local.

## Bezier and control points

The graphics variant. A cubic Bezier is defined by four points: two the curve passes through and
two it only leans towards.

```
P₀ ────────── P₁
 \              \        curve starts at P₀ heading at P₁,
  \              \       ends at P₃ arriving from P₂
   P₂ ────────── P₃
```

$$B(t) = (1-t)^3 P_0 + 3(1-t)^2 t\, P_1 + 3(1-t) t^2 P_2 + t^3 P_3, \qquad t \in [0, 1]$$

The curve stays inside the convex hull of the four points, which makes clipping and bounding
cheap, and the coefficients are the binomial weights, so the whole thing is a weighted average
that slides from $P_0$ to $P_3$. This is what a pen tool draws, what a font outline is, and what
a keyframe animation curve interpolates. Chaining Beziers with collinear handles across the join
is exactly the $C^1$ condition above, which is why dragging one handle in a vector editor moves
its partner.

## Where it turns up

- **Fonts.** TrueType uses quadratic Beziers, PostScript and OpenType CFF use cubics. Every glyph
  you are reading is a spline.
- **CAD and CNC.** NURBS, the weighted rational generalisation, is the industry surface standard.
- **Animation and easing.** `cubic-bezier()` in CSS is literally this function.
- **Data smoothing.** Smoothing splines trade exact interpolation for a roughness penalty, which
  is the same regularisation idea [[MACHINE LEARNING]] uses against overfitting.
- **Numerical work.** Interpolating a table of measurements before integrating or
  differentiating it, in [[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]] territory.

## Core facts

- One high-degree polynomial oscillates (Runge); many low-degree pieces do not.
- Knots are the joins; the class $C^k$ says how many derivatives agree there.
- Cubic is the minimum degree giving $C^2$, and $C^2$ is where the seam stops being visible.
- $n$ intervals, $4n$ unknowns, two conditions short: natural (zero end curvature) or clamped
  (fixed end slopes) closes the gap.
- The solve is a tridiagonal linear system, $O(n)$.
- Splines are **local**: moving one point changes only the neighbouring pieces.
- Bezier curves interpolate their endpoints and only approximate the interior control points.
- A Bezier stays within the convex hull of its control points.
